definition.text: A situation where a competitive market for some good would make everyone better off, yet no such market exists.

facts.text: Pollution is the classic case: a factory dumping waste into a river harms people downstream, but has no incentive to count that harm, so no market for pollution forms.
Markets can also be missing because of coordination failures such as the free-rider problem, difficulty monitoring who causes harm, high transaction costs, or lack of trust and information.
Alternative fuels show the chicken-and-egg problem: stations won't sell a fuel until such cars exist, and people won't buy the cars until stations exist.
Governments can create the missing conditions; for pollution, a popular solution is assigning property rights so the parties can bargain, as in the Coase theorem.
Economists may try to avoid waste by creating missing markets so that efficient trading can happen where none existed before.

definition.text: A state of the economy in which the mix of goods produced matches what people want, so that society's welfare is as high as it can be.

facts.text: It is reached when each good's marginal benefit to consumers is at least the marginal cost of producing it; for a firm in a perfect market this means price equals marginal cost.
With no externalities, the market equilibrium is where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost, so net social benefit is maximized.
At that point social surplus is maximized and there is no deadweight loss.
Example: at an output of 40 the marginal cost is $6 but buyers would pay $15, so the good is under-consumed; the efficient output is 70, where marginal cost equals marginal utility.
A monopoly can set price above marginal cost, making the allocation inefficient and causing a deadweight welfare loss.
When a market fails to allocate resources efficiently, through imperfect knowledge, market power or externalities, there is market failure.
Pareto efficiency is possible without allocative efficiency, when no one can gain without someone losing but gainers could gain more than losers lose.

definition.text: Kenneth Arrow's proof that no way of combining people's rankings of options into a group ranking can meet all the basic requirements of rational choice.

facts.text: In particular, no such rule can satisfy independence of irrelevant alternatives, so in voting no ranked system can fully avoid the spoiler effect.
Arrow proved the theorem in 1950, founding modern social choice theory, a branch of welfare economics that studies how to combine preferences across a society.
It generalizes Condorcet's voting paradox: with three voters and three options, the majority can prefer A to B, B to C and C to A even though each voter is consistent.
Arrow remarked that most voting systems do not work badly all the time; he only proved that all can work badly at times.
Black's median voter theorem showed that if voters and candidates lie along a single left-right spectrum, Arrow's conditions can all be met by majority rule.
The theorem depends on people giving rankings; rated voting systems that ask for scores, such as 0–10, can escape it.
By the 1950s some economists claimed the theorem proved that any attempt to build normative standards in economics was doomed.

definition.text: The principle that a choice between two options, A and B, should not depend on how anyone feels about some third, unrelated option C.

facts.text: For a voting rule, it means society's ranking of A against B should not flip just because voters change their view of A against C.
It is equivalent to saying an election should be free of spoiler candidates.
Behavioural economists have found that individuals themselves violate it, for example through decoy effects.

definition.text: A measure of income inequality, developed by the British economist Anthony Atkinson, that lets the user choose how much to care about inequality.

facts.text: Its parameter ε, the 'inequality aversion' level, makes the index more sensitive to the bottom of the income distribution as it rises.
The index gives the share of current income that could be given up, without lowering social welfare, if incomes were made perfectly equal.
It runs from 0 to 1 and is zero only when all incomes are the same; with ε = 0 (no aversion to inequality) it is always zero.
It is tied to a generalized entropy index, so overall inequality can be broken down by groups, which the Gini index cannot do.
